text.text: Similarly, cross-linguistic interference/influence (CLI) can also be understood as a process of shifting representations.
The process of CLI could arise through several mechanisms.
Firstly, the L2 input may update some of the learner's linguistic statistics, where one type of structure or construction becomes more or less frequent than it was before due to that input.

For example, languages which feature relative clause attachment ambiguity often have a preference for one of the two interpretations (high or low attachment), where one interpretation appears more frequently than the other in natural language (modulated by a number of factors, such as the type of head noun), and the preferences and proportions of each interpretation can vary widely across languages.
High and low relative clause attachment involves the same structure, but with different relationships with meaning.

When learning an L2 with a different attachment preference, the probabilistic mapping process between syntax and meaning may be sensitive to the change in statistics presented by the new language, resulting in an overall shift in attachment preferences purely as a fact of statistics.
The same effect could emerge in any linguistic phenomenon that can be influenced by statistics.
Another mechanism of CLI in M-WOW is a "tug-of-war" between representations during telophase in syntactic mitosis.

Elements that share representations at anaphase or telophase may lack sufficient evidence to suggest that they should be fully separate representations, and so all new evidence about that element would apply to the single shared representation.
The tug-of-war occurs when new evidence from the L2 leads the learner to shift that representation in one direction, while continuing exposure to the L1 provides evidence not to.
Until the element advances to cytokinesis, the bi-directional pressures will continue.
If it does move into the final stage of mitosis, the original representation may not immediately return to its original state, but remain there until enough evidence accumulates to shift it back.
The degree of conflict between representations in the L1 and L2 would also likely modulate CLI.

In attrition, conflicting representations should be more vulnerable because continued exposure to the attriting language is limited, meaning that new evidence does not come in to reinforce that representation.

In interference, conflicting representations may be less vulnerable depending on how crucial those representations are to the learner's communicative goals (comprehensibility, clarity, etc.) in each language.

If that representation is has a large role in comprehensibility (e.g., word order in English, where an ungrammatical word order would significantly impact comprehension), both of the conflicting representations would be preserved; features with a smaller role (e.g., grammatical gender in Spanish, where the intended meaning of an utterance is often recoverable even with incorrect gender markers or agreement).

When the elements that have a large role in comprehensibility in the L1 and L2 are in conflict, and both representations are reinforced through continued use, the learner would be more likely to preserve both, while those that have a smaller role in comprehensibility may be less likely to be preserved (e.g., conflicting word orders for an English speaker may be less vulnerable to CLI than conflicting grammatical gender for a Spanish speaker).
If a speaker goes long enough without speaking a language, that language can be gradually forgotten.

Similarly to language acquisition, attrition in the M-WOW model may not be uniform across language mechanisms; the language can attrite either in its entirety, or just specific features, representations, mappings, or processing strategies of the language.

Because the model assumes that each type of representation is independent, meaning, syntax, and form should be able to attrite dissociably; for example, the phonological realization of case or grammatical gender may be preserved even if the corresponding syntactic representations are not, or vice versa.

The elements or processes that are most likely to attrite are largely dependent on those that are used in the dominant language, where those that are not used in the dominant language or that conflict with those in the dominant language will attrite first.

For example, the loss or reduction of case morphology has been observed for speakers of several languages in environments where the dominant language had comparatively reduced case morphology (e.g., Finnish-English, Glodstaf et al., 2025; German-English, Altenberg, 1995; Swedish-English and Swedish-French; Håkansson, 1995).

text.text: Beyond just forgetting, an alternative avenue for language attrition made available in the M-WOW model is that the process of syntactic mitosis -normally used to acquire new representations and shift existing ones -is applied in such a way that one of the languages is not preserved (akin to the Attrition via Acquisition (AvA) model; Hicks & Dominguez, 2020).
text.formatted: Beyond just forgetting, an alternative avenue for language attrition made available in the M-WOW model is that the process of syntactic mitosis -normally used to acquire new representations and shift existing ones -is applied in such a way that one of the languages is not preserved (akin to the Attrition via Acquisition (AvA) model; <ref type="bibr">Hicks & Dominguez, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In second language acquisition, elements begin in metaphase, where the L2 form is associated with the L1 form directly, and they advance to anaphase, where the two forms are both associated with the L1 syntax.
After anaphase, representations may advance to telophase, where the syntactic representation for the L2 begins to shift and separate from the L1 syntax.

In the case of attrition, however, this could be a point of vulnerability, where instead of splitting the two syntactic representations, the single syntactic representation just shifts toward what is needed for the L2, shown in Figure 5 as "shifting".

text.text: In this situation, there is not enough sustaining evidence for the learner to justify the existence of two separate representations, so they make small, incremental changes in the syntactic representation until it eventually adds up to being catastrophic for the attrited language.

Elements that were acquired later may attrite first, assuming that the speaker may not have made as strong a commitment to those elements compared to other aspects of the language, making them more vulnerable to shifting or fading.
Thus, the speaker may fail to preserve specific grammatical features required for the attrited language, in a similar way to how in L2 acquisition learners may fail to acquire those same features.
For elements that make it to the final stage of syntactic mitosis, where the L2 syntax has fully separated from the L1 syntax, the mechanism of attrition would likely be different.
One mechanism is forgetting, where a representation is dropped from memory (akin to Ecke, 2004; Ammerlaan, 1996).
text.formatted: One mechanism is forgetting, where a representation is dropped from memory (akin to <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Ecke, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ammerlaan, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The syntax and form representations themselves may decay in memory due to lack of use, or their association with meaning and the representations of the dominant language become weakened, making them harder to retrieve but ultimately preserving their features.
The forgetting process or weakening of associations is shown in Figure 5 as "fading".
text.formatted: The forgetting process or weakening of associations is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref> as "fading".

text.text: Another mechanism could be regression, where the syntactic representations merge together again and return to anaphase, but since the learner had at one point sufficient evidence to suggest that there should be separate syntactic representations for the L1 and L2, it seems unlikely that they would merge those representations back together.
Thus, the stage that each element reaches in mitosis may be a significant factor in language attrition, in that it influences which elements or features are more vulnerable to decay.
This process would occur at the level of individual elements, rather than the language as a whole, but grammatical features like gender or case could be more broadly affected.

As shown in Figure 5, elements that are in anaphase or telophase stages of syntactic mitosis are more vulnerable to shifting, whereas elements that are at the cytokinesis stage (or have not undergone mitosis in the first place) would be more vulnerable to fading.

text.text: Consequently, representations that are cognates, involve straightforward translations, or involve similar kinds of grammatical features may be more likely to stay at anaphase or telophase, so those representations would be expected to shift to be more similar to those of the dominant language, but would not be lost altogether (e.g., speakers of Greek that live in a German-dominant community would preserve grammatical gender features because both languages have grammatical gender, but they would come to rely more heavily on the German gender features over time).

Meanwhile, representations or features that are very dissimilar from their parallel in the dominant L2 -or that do not have a parallel in the L2 -would likely have reached cytokinesis or not have gone through mitosis at all, and thus would be expected to fade due to underuse (e.g., speakers of Spanish in an English-dominant community would not be expected to preserve grammatical gender features).

If we assume that fading is a much slower process than shifting, this would explain why beginning level learners may show little recall of that language later in life because those representations were shifted, while disused intermediate or more advanced languages can show retention even after years of disuse because those representations were only subject to a slow fading process (Bahrick, 1984).

text.text: According to the critical threshold hypothesis of language attrition (Neisser, 1984), the elements of a language that are learned best are the last to attrite, whereas more complex grammatical processes (e.g., case marking and agreement in languages like Estonian or Hungarian, which involves adding morphemes and/or linear reordering based on non-adjacent morphosyntactic relationships, as well as local agreement processes) are harder to learn and thus are the first to be lost.

text.text: In a non-lexicalist framework, grammatical elements or processes that are more complex can be thought of as harder to acquire because they involve more steps to generate them or transform them appropriately.

Conversely, these grammatical elements may also be more vulnerable to attrition because any step could individually be affected by the processes of shifting or fading, leading to catastrophic results for the whole process.
The effects of shifting and fading may be identifiable in implicit measures such as priming effects or ERP responses.

For example, the process of shifting causes some representations to become more like that of the L2 than the L1, and thus those representations may be primed by different features, and may change which language is more dominant in those priming effects (e.g., the gender priming effect observed in Salamoura & Williams (2007) would shift to preference the gender feature of the L2 rather than the L1 over the course of attrition).

This model of attrition that M-WOW makes available can account for some data from heritage speakers.
For example, heritage Spanish speakers that have a dominant language of English often have difficulties with grammatical gender.

If the syntactic representations for Spanish were shifted toward English, rather than split, they would ultimately lose the grammatical gender feature on nouns, perhaps with some variability across items.

They also tend to struggle with the subjunctive in Spanish (Giancaspro, 2019), a feature that also appears in English, but it is not an inflectional form as it is in Spanish and has a somewhat different distribution (Waller, 2017).
text.formatted: They also tend to struggle with the subjunctive in Spanish <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Giancaspro, 2019)</ref>, a feature that also appears in English, but it is not an inflectional form as it is in Spanish and has a somewhat different distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">(Waller, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Because of the misalignment between the subjunctive in English and Spanish, bilinguals could not rely on the English subjunctive as a foundation for the Spanish subjunctive, and would likely need to develop separate representations; if heritage speakers' representation of the subjunctive has shifted toward English, or their representation of the Spanish subjunctive has faded, they will struggle to produce the subjunctive in Spanish like Spanish-dominant speakers.

As another example, heritage Korean speakers with English as their dominant language use bare noun constructions less than Korean-dominant speakers, preferring the more English-like demonstrative (Seo & Kuza, 2024).
text.formatted: As another example, heritage Korean speakers with English as their dominant language use bare noun constructions less than Korean-dominant speakers, preferring the more English-like demonstrative <ref type="bibr">(Seo & Kuza, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, as the Korean proficiency of the heritage speakers improves, their performance becomes more like Korean-dominant speakers, suggesting that the processes of shifting and fading are not irreversible, and that those states can become the starting point for a new process of syntactic mitosis.
Our model of attrition may also provide insights into language contact and change beyond the level of the individual.

In one case study on the endangered languages of the Ryukyuan islands in Japan, it has been observed that younger generations of speakers do not use politeness markers, even though the dominant language of Japanese also has grammatical politeness markers (van der Lubbe et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In one case study on the endangered languages of the Ryukyuan islands in Japan, it has been observed that younger generations of speakers do not use politeness markers, even though the dominant language of Japanese also has grammatical politeness markers <ref type="bibr">(van der Lubbe et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although this initially would seem to be in conflict with our account of language attrition -both languages have grammatical politeness, so why should the non-dominant language lose its politeness markers? -it can be understood instead as the consequence of shifting rather than fading.

Because Japanese provides a more dominant set of politeness markers, the younger speakers may lack sufficient input to progress through the stages of syntactic mitosis with those of their heritage language, and thus do not acquire them.

The context of use also plays a role in this process, where Japanese is the language primarily used in formal contexts for those speakers, while their heritage language may be used in typically less formal contexts.
Thus, the consequence of this process is the shifting of politeness markers at a community level to be more Japanese-like.

The possibility of "shifting" and "fading" as possible side effects in the syntactic mitosis process suggests that there may be general vulnerability in the process, and that learners may make a mistake in the process that could be catastrophic for their L1 or influence it in some other way; in normal second language acquisition, continued exposure to the L1 would help to prevent or correct those kinds of errors.

text.text: The non-lexicalist approach of M-WOW offers testable predictions about patterns of impairment, assessment, recovery, and treatment that can guide future research in aphasia and dementia.
In M-WOW, impairment in aphasia or dementia does not necessarily affect the entire language system equally.

Instead, patients can exhibit selective impairments to representations (e.g., phonology; Astell & Harley, 1996; Goodglass et al., 1976; Middleton & Schwartz, 2013), to the mapping processes between representations during processing, to language control, or some combination of the three.

text.text: Damage to a representation should affect the tasks and languages that recruit that representation, while damage to a mapping should affect the processing operations that depend on that mapping, potentially producing dissociations between comprehension and production.

Impaired language control should produce disproportionate difficulty under conditions requiring selection between languages, inhibition or facilitation of competing alternatives, or increased cognitive control.

These deficits may not be immediately transparent; deficits that appear to reflect impaired linguistic representations may instead be caused by impairments in the mappings between meaning, syntax, and phonological form, particularly when these processes depend on cognitive control.
Testing these predictions requires assessment of the same syntactic structures across languages and tasks that recruit different representations, mappings, and control processes.
Predicted mechanisms of the impacts of a brain injury and potential mechanisms of recovery.

The left panel shows an example of a representation that has reached cytokinesis prior to injury, though multiple configurations and stages of syntactic mitosis would also be possible and influence the outcomes in aphasia and recovery.

The middle panel shows an example of two possible mechanisms of language impairment: representation disruption, where the representations themselves are impacted, and mapping disruption, where the mapping process which links different levels of representation are affected.
Different levels of representation or mapping processes would be affected differently depending on the location of the brain injury, and each language may be affected to different degrees.

The right panel illustrates potential pathways for recovery (green lines): change in reliance, where existing mappings are re-strengthened to compensate for a missing representation, and restoration of access, where existing or recovered mappings are re-strengthened to allow those representations to be accessed.
These pathways show hypothesized recovery-related changes, rather than the immediate effects of neurological injury.
Aphasia may not necessarily affect both of a bilingual's languages equally.

Case reports have described the re-emergence of a seldom-used language after stroke (Leemann et al., 2007) and increased reliance on an earlier acquired language in dementia (McMurtray et al., 2009), though M-WOW suggests that there should also be effects at the level of individual linguistic consider the specific linguistic properties shared between languages rather than treating generalization as an all-or-none outcome.

text.text: Patients with impaired language control may instead benefit from treatment targeting language selection and competition.
For example, Ansaldo et al. (2010) demonstrated improvement in a bilingual patient with pathological language mixing by teaching a strategy to recognize and correct involuntary language switching.

text.text: Similar approaches could potentially be extended to sentence production by training patients to select and maintain the intended language when producing syntactic structures that differ across their languages.
Treatment could also manipulate language switching demands and cross-language interference to determine whether improvements reflect better control over competing representations.
However, the effects of these approaches on syntactic production and cross-language generalization have not been established.
The M-WOW framework also generates predictions about recovery patterns in bilingual aphasia.
We propose that recovery may involve changes to the organization of the bilingual language system itself, rather than exclusively restoring the premorbid organization.

During recovery, patients may shift their reliance on different syntactic representations or mappings to compensate for those that are impaired, potentially producing changes in the relative contributions of L1 and L2.

This could be investigated through cross-language structural priming, interference, and patterns of generalization to untrained constructions, where we might expect to observe changes even on structures that were not directly treated.

Change in the direction or magnitude of cross-language structural priming for untrained constructions could indicate changes in which representations are recruited, particularly if it persists across tasks and processing demands.
Access to previously available representations may also be restored by recruiting existing mappings, allowing them to be accessed via a different route.
These possible recovery pathways are illustrated in the right panel of Figure 6.
text.formatted: These possible recovery pathways are illustrated in the right panel of Figure <ref type="figure">6</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal changes in performance may reflect the recovery of previously impaired components, changes in access to preserved components, or representational reorganization during recovery, where the relationship between the L1 and L2 may change over time.

Recovery is also expected to vary depending on each element's degree of representational overlap, providing an account of how recovery may be non-uniform across languages or tasks even when some underlying representations are shared.
If a particular syntactic representation is recruited in both languages, recovery of that representation should benefit both languages.

Consequently, recovery should be relatively parallel for structures with shared representations, although the magnitude of improvement may differ depending on premorbid proficiency, language use, and the status of the mappings supporting each language.
In contrast, structures with independent representations may recover separately, resulting in differential recovery of L1 and L2.
Partially overlapping representations may show intermediate or inconsistent patterns of recovery.

Recovery of mappings or language control may produce other patterns; for example, recovery of the syntax-form mapping may improve production without equivalent changes in comprehension, while improvements in language control may benefit several structures or both languages.

In this paper, we have outlined three desiderata of a non-lexicalist model of multilingualism: that the language system should be probabilistic and context-dependent, that there should be no strict divide between languages in the bilingual mind, and that language acquisition should not have to progress uniformly, while also being able to accommodate a diverse set of experiences, and being testable and falsifiable.

From these criteria, we developed the M-WOW model of bilingual language production, which is able to capture a wider range of linguistic phenomena from many different languages and language families, and also can also accommodate many aspects of the bilingual experience, including sequential and simultaneous second language acquisition, changes in representations over the course of language acquisition, and language attrition.
We also describe the process of syntactic mitosis and how it may be involved during language attrition, as well as in cross-linguistic interference and bilingual aphasia.

Although M-WOW is more computationally expensive and complex than other models like Multilink or the RHM, we think this is justified given the evidence that needs to be accounted for, as well as the explanatory power that this new model provides.
elements.
Each language could be affected differently based on whether the representations or the mappings were affected, as well as the stage of syntactic mitosis that each element has reached.

Elements that share a representation across languages should exhibit similar patterns of impairment when the shared representation is damaged, while elements that have reached cytokinesis may be affected differently between languages if one set of representations is impaired more than the other.
Meanwhile, when the representations themselves are preserved while their mappings to other representations are impaired, the deficits need not be parallel.

Impaired mapping processes or language control may cause differences between languages depending on the complexity of the mapping process and how much cognitive control it requires, as well as the other kinds of mappings that are still available.

Because not all items within the same category will necessarily have been at the same stage of syntactic mitosis prior to the injury, especially for more beginner or intermediate speakers of an L2, we would expect that a patient's performance across different items within a category may be inconsistent, where the same kind of impairment would result in different outcomes for those items.

text.text: Adopting M-WOW could therefore improve assessment in bilingual aphasia.

First, assessments should consider the likely status of individual representations prior to neurologic injury or disease, including premorbid proficiency and language history (see Fahey et al., 2026; Gray & Kiran, 2013; Kiran & Roberts, 2012), to estimate the degree of representational overlap in individual elements across the patient's languages.

text.text: Second, assessments should examine the same representations through different processing pathways to distinguish damage to representations from damage to the mappings.

For example, relatively preserved comprehension of a structure alongside impaired production could suggest that the syntactic representation is intact while the syntax-form mapping is impaired, while impairment across several tasks recruiting the same representation could be consistent with representational damage.
Assessments should also manipulate processing demands to identify possible impairments in language control.
These could include tasks involving language interference, switching, or competing syntactic alternatives, as well as comparisons across levels of syntactic complexity.
If performance deteriorates disproportionately with increased control demands, this may indicate that the deficits are not exclusively representational.
In sum, appropriate assessment requires more than comparing general language impairment in L1 and L2, and should include converging evidence from multiple tasks analyzing individual elements.

The resulting assessment profile should inform treatment selection by identifying whether intervention should target the impaired syntactic representations, the mappings required to access them, and/or language control.
Treatment following the M-WOW framework should target the specific locus of impairment.

If syntactic representations are impaired, treatment could explicitly train the relevant syntactic structures, such as noncanonical sentences involving syntactic movement, as in Treatment of Underlying Forms (TUF; Thompson & Shapiro, 2005).
